content: Professor Emmanuelle Cambau received funding from Hain Life Science to conduct research exclusively on genotypic mutations that confer resistance to rare mycobacteria, including Mycobacterium leprae. It was determined that this funding would not influence discussions related to diagnostics. Consequently, this interest was not considered a conflict, and Professor Cambau was allowed to participate as an expert in the Guideline Development Group (GDG). Professor Travis Porco disclosed that part of his salary in 2016 was supported by the Novartis Foundation. Upon clarification, it was noted that while his institute received funding from the Novartis Foundation for the Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTD) Modeling Consortium, which examines the burden of leprosy and the impact of public health interventions, only $1,000 of this funding contributed to his salary. This interest was deemed unrelated to the subject matter of the guidelines. Furthermore, the funding ceased in 2016, and no further proposals for funding were submitted by him or his employer, the University of California. Therefore, this interest was not considered a conflict, and Professor Porco was permitted to participate as a GDG expert. Professor W. Cairns Smith was asked to provide additional information regarding funding he received from the Novartis Foundation to attend the International Leprosy Congress in Beijing, China, in September 2016. He clarified that the funding came from the Novartis Foundation, not Novartis Pharmaceuticals. Over four years (2013–2017), he received a total of £8,000 for travel, which is below the WHO DOI policy threshold of $5,000 per year for significant financial interest. This interest was not considered a conflict, and Professor Smith was allowed to participate as a GDG expert. Dr. Willem (Pim) Kuipers received funding from the Leprosy Research Initiative (LRI) through his role as a researcher at Griffith University, Queensland, Australia. The LRI is funded solely by NGOs, with no involvement from pharmaceutical or for-profit companies. This interest was not considered a conflict, and Dr. Kuipers was allowed to participate as a GDG expert. Dr. Marcos da Cunha Lopes Virmond received $300 from the Novartis Foundation in August 2015 to attend an international leprosy conference. This amount is below the $5,000 threshold defined by the WHO DOI policy for significant financial interest. Based on these considerations, this interest was not considered a conflict, and Dr. Virmond was allowed to participate as a GDG expert. Mrs. Marivic F. Balagon received a grant of $164,349 from the Novartis Foundation to field-test a diagnostic test for leprosy. She also received €292,276 from the LRI through the National Infectious Disease Center of the Philippines to co-fund the same study and an additional €109,223 to test a nerve function monitoring tool. Dr. Davis Hughes has been employed by Novartis Pharmaceuticals since 2011. Dr. Shengelia Bakhuti has been employed by the Novartis Foundation since 2015. Professor Eliane Ignotti received a grant of 82,000 Swiss francs from the Novartis Foundation to conduct the LPEP study in Brazil and to attend the annual meeting of the research multicountry project on post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for leprosy with single-dose rifampicin (SDR) in 2016. Dr. Herman-Joseph Kawuma has been employed by the German Tuberculosis and Leprosy Relief Association, an NGO providing leprosy care services. He was a member of WHO’s Technical Advisory Group on Leprosy until June 2016 and is currently a member of the Regional Programme Review Group on case management of NTDs in the WHO African Region. Professor Jan Hendrik Richardus received funding from the Novartis Foundation between 2014 and 2017 to conduct research on post-exposure prophylaxis through his supervisory role in the LPEP multicountry study and as part of the NTD Modeling Consortium (€860,000). A portion of this grant (€330,000) was provided by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation through the Novartis Foundation. Dr. Wim van Brakel declared that the organization he worked for, Netherlands Leprosy Relief, received a grant of €300,000 between 2014 and 2017 to conduct a pilot project on post-exposure prophylaxis for leprosy with SDR in India and Indonesia as part of the multicountry LPEP study. Dr. Amudha Poobalan, who conducted systematic reviews of evidence at the University of Aberdeen, declared no conflict of interest and did not participate in formulating policy recommendations. Regarding diagnostic tests for leprosy, the WHO has historically recommended diagnosis based on at least one of three cardinal signs: hypopigmented skin patches with sensory loss, enlarged nerves, or slit-skin smears positive for leprosy bacilli. However, studies on diagnostic tests, including those using blood or serum samples, have been conducted. Tests such as ELISA, immunochromatographic/lateral flow tests, PCR, and combined antibody/cytokine tests have been evaluated. Despite some promising results, no test has demonstrated sufficient sensitivity and specificity, particularly for paucibacillary (PB) leprosy. PCR on skin biopsy specimens shows relatively higher sensitivity and very high specificity but is not feasible outside referral or research centers due to technical complexity and lack of commercially available tests. The evidence for diagnostic accuracy is of very low quality, and there is significant uncertainty about the impact of diagnostic accuracy on clinical outcomes. The cost-effectiveness of these tests is difficult to estimate due to a lack of data on costs and clinical outcomes. Additionally, stakeholders may be reluctant to implement laboratory tests that are more expensive than clinical examinations or other tests like smears. Feasibility is higher in referral centers, but drawing blood may be simpler than performing slit-skin smears or biopsies.
